paragraphs.text: We investigated the impact of oxygen on a strictly anaerobic, methanogenic benzene-degrading enrichment culture derived decades ago from oil-contaminated sediment. The culture includes a benzene fermenter from Deltaproteobacteria candidate clade Sva0485 (referred to as ORM2) and methanogenic archaea. A one-time injection of 0.1 mL air , simulating a small leak into 30 mL batch culture bottle, had no measurable impact on benzene degradation rates, although retrospectively, a tiny enrichment of aerobic taxa was detected. A subsequent 100 times larger injection of air stalled methanogenesis and caused drastic perturbation of the microbial community. A benzene-degrading Pseudomonas became highly enriched and consumed all available oxygen. Anaerobic benzene-degrading ORM2 cell numbers plummeted during this time; re-growth and associated recovery of methanogenic benzene degradation took almost 1 year. These results highlight the oxygen sensitivity of this methanogenic culture and confirm that the mechanism for anaerobic biotransformation of benzene is independent of oxygen, fundamentally different from established aerobic pathways, and is carried out by distinct microbial communities. The study also highlights the importance of including microbial decay in characterizing and modeling mixed microbial communities.
Methanogenic benzene degradation in a highly enriched anaerobic consortium was inhibited for 1 year after transient exposure to oxygen, attributed to mass decay of benzene-fermenting bacteria.

paragraphs.section: Introduction
paragraphs.text: Benzene is a widespread and toxic pollutant notorious for its persistence in anaerobic environments, including contaminated aquifers and deep sediments. Once thought to be completely recalcitrant in the absence of molecular oxygen, the anaerobic transformation of [14C] benzene to labeled CO2 was first demonstrated in the aftermath of the Amoco Cadiz oil spill in 1980.1 Years later, this methanogenic activity was reproduced in several laboratory-scale experiments.2−6 Oxidation of [14C] benzene to labeled CO2 was also stoichiometrically linked to the reduction of ferric iron,7,8 nitrate,9,10 and sulfate6,7,11−13 catalyzed by a handful of specialized microorganisms.14,15 Although enzymatic mechanism(s) for benzene activation are still not fully understood, proposed oxygen-independent transformation reactions include hydroxylation,3,16,17 carboxylation,17−20 or through a Wood–Ljungdahl-like pathway, yielding benzoyl-CoA.21 The existence of at least two different activation mechanisms is predicted from stable isotope fractionation experiments.22

paragraphs.section: Introduction
paragraphs.text: Benzene biodegradation proceeds more readily under aerobic conditions23 and is usually preferred for bioremediation applications. In the subsurface, the caveat becomes supplying enough oxygen to drive complete benzene attenuation. Low permeability contaminated aquifers rapidly deplete dissolved O2, creating anaerobic zones where benzene remains recalcitrant. In situ injection of oxygen is inefficient, as O2 is poorly soluble in water and demand from contaminants and other reduced species is usually high. Other technologies such as traditional excavation or pump-and-treat strategies are costly and disruptive to the site, and they are not always feasible at large or deep sites. Recent studies have proposed injecting other agents such as nanoparticles (e.g., metal peroxides, zero-valent iron) into the zone of contamination,24−26 but these can be limited by difficulties in distribution, aggregation, maintaining activity, and cost. In the end, anaerobic bioremediation may be a more economical and sustainable strategy for such locations. Decontamination can be achieved anaerobically by stimulating the growth of certain native microorganisms, which can degrade contaminants (biostimulation) or by adding exogenous culture (bioaugmentation).15,27−30

paragraphs.section: Introduction
paragraphs.text: Perhaps ironically, one frequently asked question is whether successful benzene bioremediation can truly be independent of oxygen. This skepticism is in part due to the chemical stability of its unsubstituted aromatic ring and the long history of difficulties cultivating anaerobic benzene-degrading cultures.31 Several reports of oxygen-generating reactions in an otherwise anoxic environment also contribute to this apprehension.32−36 For example, nitrate and chlorate dismutation reactions have been shown to generate molecular oxygen internally that can then be used in benzene activation with powerful O2-dependent oxygenases.32,33,37 However, mono- and dioxygenase genes and associated aerobic pathways have never been detected in the metagenomes of some benzene-degrading anaerobic cultures.18,20,21,38 Others have suggested that reactions with iron can generate radical oxygen species that may oxidize benzene.19 While this can occur, it is highly unlikely to drive benzene degradation at consistent rates and stoichiometry indefinitely, especially in longstanding enrichment cultures.15,20,38

paragraphs.section: Introduction
paragraphs.text: Overall, more lines of evidence that anaerobic benzene degradation can be a strictly anoxic process are needed, and by extension, a greater understanding of how oxygen affects the activity and composition of anaerobic benzene-degrading consortia. We investigated these research questions by adding small volumes of air into microcosms containing an active methanogenic benzene-degrading enrichment culture, simulating a leaking bottle cap. This 27-year-old enrichment culture lineage and its key benzene-degrading bacterium (ORM2, an unclassified member of the Deltaproteobacteria candidate clade Sva0485) were recently described in detail in Toth et al.15 Nearly identical 16S rRNA gene sequences to ORM2 have also been found in benzene-degrading methanogenic cultures from Japan39,40 and in microcosms from China.41 From our results, we determined that oxygen in the added air stimulated the growth of a benzene-degrading Pseudomonas that was previously undetectable in the consortium. Exposure to oxygen also resulted in dramatic reductions (1–2 orders of magnitude) of ORM2 and other bacteria and archaea vital to this culture. After anoxic conditions were re-established, it took almost 1 year for methanogenic benzene degradation to recover, attributed to the rapid decay of ORM2 cells and subsequent long doubling times to re-establish their initial (pre-oxygen) concentrations. These data clearly refute any possible involvement of oxygen in benzene activation by ORM2.

paragraphs.section:
Materials and
Methods/Methanogenic Benzene-Degrading Culture DGG-B
paragraphs.text: DGG-B is a large-scale culture lineage of the OR consortium, a lab-scale methanogenic benzene-degrading consortium enriched from an oil refinery in Oklahoma.15,42 Large-scale DGG-B cultures are grown at SiREM laboratories (Guelph, ON) in 100 L stainless steel vessels containing a defined anaerobic mineral medium,43 and benzene as their sole carbon and energy source (aqueous concentration of 25 mg/L, ∼32 mmol per vessel). Benzene is refed to DGG-B as needed, usually once every 4–6 weeks. The growth medium contains 0.44 mg/L (500 μM) of amorphous iron sulfide (FeS) as a reducing agent and 1 mg/L resazurin as a redox indicator. Resazurin is clear (i.e., colorless) when fully reduced (<−51 mV—a potential at which no oxygen remains) but turns bright pink (oxidized form) at higher redox potentials. DGG-B is currently undergoing bench-scale and field-scale testing to evaluate its potential for bioaugmentation of benzene-contaminated groundwater.15

paragraphs.section:
Materials and
Methods/Experimental Setup and
Sampling
paragraphs.text: In May 2017, an aliquot (∼1 L) of DGG-B was transported in a sealed bottle from SiREM to the University of Toronto for testing. Culture portions (30 mL) were dispensed into twenty-three 40 mL clear glass screw cap bottles and amended with neat benzene (4.1 μmol/bottle) for an initial aqueous concentration of 10 mg/L. Bottles were sealed with Teflon mininert screw caps and incubated in a Coy anaerobic glovebox (supplied with 10% H2, 10% CO2, and 80% N2) at room temperature (∼23 °C). Benzene depletion and methane formation were monitored, and bottles were reamended with benzene whenever concentrations dropped below 5 mg/L. After 9 months of monitoring all bottles, five bottles (designated Bottles 1–5) with similar and consistent benzene degradation rates (∼0.3 μmol/bottle/day or about 0.8 mg/L/day) were selected for inclusion in oxygen experiments.

paragraphs.section:
Materials and
Methods/Experimental Setup and
Sampling
paragraphs.text: Experimental treatments for each bottle are provided in Table 1. Day 0 of the experiment was March 19, 2018, when each of the 5 similar bottles was refed and closer monitoring began. Bottles 1–3 were amended with an initial 0.1 mL dose of room air (∼78% N2 and 21% O2) on day 39 or 53 of this experiment by syringe injection. Subsequently, Bottles 1 and 2 received one (Bottle 1, day 94) or two (Bottle 2, days 94 and 224) additional, successive doses of approximately 10 mL of air (Table 1). This was achieved by removing the bottles from the glovebox and briefly opening (for 15 s) their bottle caps to replace the headspace volume with air. As illustrated in Figure 1, the addition of 10 mL air made the resazurin in the culture medium turn pink. Depletion of all available O2 was indicated by resazurin returning to its colorless (reduced) form. Two bottles served as positive controls (Bottles 4 and 5) and were maintained exclusively in the glovebox without being exposed to oxygen. Bottle 6 (medium-only) was prepared as an anaerobic sterile control and was exposed to 10 mL of air on day 16. Active bottles were incubated for up to 1225 days.

paragraphs.section:
Materials and
Methods/DNA Extraction
and Molecular Analyses
paragraphs.text: Bottles 1–5 were routinely sampled for molecular analyses. Cell pellets (10,000g centrifugation, 15 min) from 1 mL of culture were frozen at −80 °C for later DNA extraction using the DNeasy PowerSoil Kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer’s procedure. Concentrations of extracted DNA were verified using a Nanodrop ND-1000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

paragraphs.section:
Materials and
Methods/DNA Extraction
and Molecular Analyses
paragraphs.text: DNA samples were assayed by quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) using previously established primer pairs for total bacteria, total Archaea, ORM2, and Candidatus nealsonbacteria (previously referred to as OD1 and Parcubacteria, Table S1). Amplification of targeted genes was carried out in duplicate 20 μL reactions containing 10 μL of SsoFast EvaGreen Supermix (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA), 2 μL of DNA template, 500 nM of each designated forward and reverse primer, and UV-treated UltraPure distilled water (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Serial dilutions of plasmids containing corresponding 16S rRNA gene fragments were used to generate standard curves. qPCR reactions were performed using a CFX96 real-time thermal cycler (Bio-Rad Laboratories) using the following thermocycling conditions: an initial denaturation step at 98 °C for 2 min, 40 cycles of 98 °C for 5 s and annealing/extension (see Table S1) for 10 s, followed by melt curve analysis (65–95 °C with an increase of 0.5 °C every 5 s). qPCR results were processed with CFX Manager software (Bio-Rad Laboratories).

paragraphs.section:
Materials and
Methods/DNA Extraction
and Molecular Analyses
paragraphs.text: Finally, aliquots of DNA extracts were shipped on dry ice to the Genome Quebec Innovation Centre for Illumina MiSeq 300PE (paired-end) 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing. All amplicon sequence reads were generated using modified, “staggered end” 16S rRNA gene primers 926F and 1392R (Table S1), as described in Toth et al.15 Read processing and sequencing analyses were performed in QIIME 2 version 2020.11.44 The SILVA SSU 132 database45 was used to classify the resulting amplicon sequence variants (ASVs). ASVs with the same taxonomy were ranked by abundance, where ASV1 is the most abundant sequence variant recovered across all DNA samples. Two sequence variants (ASV IDs c0bc311ae7b8da92ad4208a5c83926bf and 29ca2edb9ec3825021ea0fc78298c83c) were reclassified from Candidatus Yanofskybacteria to Ca. Nealsonbacteria based on matching nucleotides sequences to a complete (closed) genome recovered from the DGG-B/OR consortium46 (available in JGI/IMG, taxon ID 2791354853). Raw amplicon sequence reads from this study were deposited into the National Center for Biotechnology Short Read Archive (SRA) under BioProject PRJNA807302.

paragraphs.section:
Materials and
Methods/Analytical Procedures
paragraphs.text: Headspace samples (300 μL) from experimental bottles were injected into a Hewlett-Packard 5890 Series II gas chromatograph equipped with GSQ 30 m × 0.53 mm I. D. PLOT column (J & W Scientific) and a flame ionization detector (GC-FID) to quantify benzene and methane, as previously described.38 Benzene and methane concentrations were monitored over time in Bottles 1–6, from before exposure to air until after methanogenic benzene degradation had resumed; all data are provided in Table S2.

paragraphs.section:
Materials and
Methods/Microbial Data Analysis
paragraphs.text: Results from qPCR analyses (16S rRNA gene copies of targeted microbial groups per mL culture) and 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing (overall community compositions over time) are summarized in Tables S3 and S4a–d. We also estimated the absolute abundance of all ASVs detected in this study by taking the total absolute bacterial or archaeal abundance from qPCR multiplied by the relative abundance within each domain from amplicon sequencing (Tables S5 and S6). Abundances measured using taxon-specific qPCR were similar to abundance estimated from multiplying general bacteria or archaea qPCR results by the relative abundance obtained from amplicon sequencing. Concentrations (in 16S rRNA gene copies/mL over time) of the most abundant ASVs in select bottles are highlighted in the main text figures (Figures 2 and 3), and for all other active bottles and major ASVs in Supporting Figures. The amplicon sequence of one ASV of interest (Pseudomonas ASV1, 466 bp) was used to build a maximum likelihood tree in Geneious 8.1.9 using a GTRGAMMA model and 100 bootstrap replicates.

paragraphs.section:
Results and Discussion/Methanogenic Benzene Degradation and Microbial
Growth in Bottles
Not Exposed to Oxygen
paragraphs.text: DGG-B cultures in Bottles 4 and 5 were maintained as usual in the anaerobic glovebox, without exposure to oxygen. As shown in Figures 2a and S1a, benzene was repeatedly degraded over the 422 days monitoring period, increasing in rate from 0.8 mg/L/day (10.2 μM/day) to 6 mg/L/day (76.9 μM/day). In the first 200 days, the ratio of methane produced to benzene consumed averaged 3.5 ± 0.1 mol/mol (Table S2), nearly identical to the expected stoichiometry shown in eq 1, where benzene (C6H6) is converted to methane (CH4), CO2 and cells (C5H7O2N). Similar ratios have been previously reported for consortia maintained in our laboratory38,43 and elsewhere.6,40 After 200 days, measured methane concentrations began to plateau and were underestimated due to pressure buildup and associated losses from sampling.1

paragraphs.section:
Results and Discussion/Methanogenic Benzene Degradation and Microbial
Growth in Bottles
Not Exposed to Oxygen
paragraphs.text: Dominant microbial phylotypes in the DGG-B/OR consortium include Deltaproteobacteria candidate clade Sva0485 (ORM2), acetoclastic Methanosaeta, and hydrogenotrophic Methanoregula that are required for the complete biodegradation of benzene to CH4 and CO2.15,21,38 A member of the Candidate phyla radiation (Ca. Nealsonbacteria, previously referred to as OD1 and Parcubacteria) has also been consistently found in the culture15,38 and is thought to be involved in biomass recycling.46 The absolute abundance of targeted microbial groups was tracked by qPCR and is shown in Figure 2b (Bottle 4) and Figure S1b (Bottle 5). 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing identified three dominant ASVs in these bottles; Sva0485 Deltaproteobacteria ASV1 (ORM2), Methanosaeta ASV1, and Methanoregula ASV1 (Figures 2c and S1c, Tables S5, and S6). Other high-abundance ASVs belonged to Ca. Nealsonbacteria and Ca. Omnitrophica (previously referred to as OP3), a candidate phylum that may also be implicated in biomass recycling47 (Figures 2c and S1c, Tables S3, and S5). Overall, the observed benzene degradation rates and growth of key consortium members (ORM2, methanogens, and candidate phyla) in these positive control bottles were as expected.

paragraphs.section:
Results and Discussion/Benzene
Biodegradation Following Oxygen Exposure
paragraphs.text: In experimental bottles, the impacts of exposure to oxygen are summarized in Table 1 and illustrated in Figure 3a (Bottle 2), Figures S2a and S3a (Bottles 1 and 3). After the first addition of 0.1 mL air, the culture medium remained colorless, indicating that the resazurin had not oxidized. There was also no observable impact on benzene degradation rate or methane production, as seen by the data from Bottle 3 (Figure S3). We surmised that the FeS used to reduce the culture medium (15 μmol/bottle) scavenged all added O2 (∼0.9 μmol/bottle) and that exceeding the oxygen demand from FeS (34 μmol/bottle) would be necessary to elicit a change in benzene degradation activity (calculations shown in Table S7). The headspace volume of the bottles was 10 mL. We reasoned that if we simply opened the bottle cap for a few seconds, we would effectively replace the headspace volume with air. Using this approach, we added ∼10 mL of air (∼86 μmol/bottle of O2) once to Bottle 1, twice to Bottle 2, and once to medium-only (sterile) Bottle 6 (Table 1). The culture medium immediately turned pink and remained pink for up to 70 days in live replicates (Figures 3a, S2a, and S4). No methane production was observed for as long as the resazurin remained pink, but benzene degradation was able to proceed in Bottles 1 and 2 following a brief (1 week) lag period. Benzene degradation eventually stopped after 61–70 days, coinciding with the resazurin returning to its reduced, colorless form (indicating that all oxygen was depleted—see Table S7 for calculations). After adding a second 10 mL of air to Bottle 2, benzene degradation resumed for 35 days until O2 was depleted once again (Figure 3a). No benzene loss was detected in Bottle 6 after oxygen was added (Figure S4). A moles balance comparing benzene degraded during the aerobic “pink” period to the amount of available oxygen in each bottle confirmed that observed benzene depletion after adding air to the bottles was coupled to oxygen consumption (Table S7).

paragraphs.section:
Results and Discussion/Benzene
Biodegradation Following Oxygen Exposure
paragraphs.text: Following oxygen depletion, we continued to monitor Bottles 1 and 2 to determine if and when anaerobic benzene degradation would recover. Methane production began slowly over several months, and finally, methanogenic benzene degradation was measurable again by day 583 in Bottle 1 and by day 666 in Bottle 2 (Figures 3a and S2a and Table 1). This lag of 323–325 days was much longer than expected, even considering the known slow doubling time of ∼30 days for ORM2.15,38,43 This prompted us to take a closer look at the microbes in each bottle over time.

paragraphs.section:
Results and Discussion/Appearance of Pseudomonas upon Exposure to
Oxygen
paragraphs.text: 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing data revealed that an ASV affiliated with Pseudomonas became the dominant taxon in Bottles 1 and 2 immediately after adding 10 mL of air (Figures 3b,c and S2b,c). Using Bottle 2 as an example, concentrations of Pseudomonas ASV1 copies/mL increased rapidly in the presence of oxygen (up to 1.2 × 109 copies/mL) but decayed very slowly under anoxic conditions (Figure 3b). It took until day 1207 for concentrations of Pseudomonas ASV1 to fall below detectable limits. Looking closely at Bottle 3, we can see transient, low abundances of Pseudomonas ASV1 (3.8 x 104 copies/mL) appear after the first 0.1 mL injection of air, even though no perturbation of the culture was observed (Figure S3b). Pseudomonas have not previously been detected in the DGG-B/OR consortium,15,38,43 and no ASVs associated with Pseudomonas were ever detected in anoxic controls Bottles 4 and 5 (Table S4a). This ASV was likely not a contaminant from the air or growth medium used because benzene losses were never detected in sterile control Bottle 6 (Table 1 and Figure S4). Pseudomonas ASV1 is closely related (100% sequence identity) to several Pseudomonas stutzeri isolates (Figure S5), although a longer 16S rRNA gene sequence (>466 base pairs) or genome is needed to verify taxonomy. P. stutzeri species are metabolically versatile and can use oxygen or nitrate as a terminal electron acceptor.48 A handful of strains are also capable of mineralizing aromatic hydrocarbons.49−51 Considering the above, benzene-degrading Pseudomonas likely persisted below detection in the DGG-B culture and were responsible for the aerobic benzene metabolism seen in Bottles 1 and 2 (Figures 3a and S2a). It is unclear how Pseudomonas have managed to persist for years in this culture lineage.

paragraphs.section: Results and Discussion/Impact of Oxygen on ORM2 and Methanogens
paragraphs.text: The microbial community composition and absolute abundance of ORM2, Archaea, and bacteria tracked in anoxic controls Bottles 4 and 5 provide a reference against which oxygen-impacted Bottles 1–3 were compared (Figures 2, 3, and S1–S3). Prior to the addition of air, concentrations of ORM2 in Bottle 3 (9.5 × 107 copies/mL) were comparable to those measured in anoxic control Bottles 4 and 5 (Table S3). After adding 10 mL of air to Bottles 1 and 2, concentrations of ORM2 steeply decreased by up to 2 orders of magnitude (Figures 3b and S2b). The addition of only 0.1 mL of air in Bottle 3 may even have resulted in a small (53%) decrease in concentrations of ORM2 (Table S3). We were surprised to see that ORM2 concentrations continued to decline in Bottles 1 and 2 long after the bottles turned from pink to colorless (i.e., bottles were devoid of O2). The lowest concentrations of ORM2 measured were 2.9 × 106 copies/mL on day 401 in Bottle 1 (Figure S2b) and 2.0 × 105 copies/mL on day 401 in Bottle 2 (Figure 3b). Both concentrations are below the estimated threshold concentrations of ORM2 (4.3 × 106 ORM2 copies/mL) needed for measurable benzene loss in batch cultures of DGG-B.15 Concentrations of total Archaea also declined up to 1 order of magnitude between days 98 and 585 (Figures 3b and S2b). Growth of the aforementioned Pseudomonas led to a 56–80% increase in total bacteria despite the rapid decay of ORM2 (Tables S3 and S5). Upon O2 depletion in Bottles 1 and 2, Pseudomonas copies began to decrease, yet it still took a further 140–240 days to see net increases in ORM2 copies. This prompted us to take a closer look at the observed growth and decay rates. Transient oxygen exposure had a prolonged negative impact on the microbial community structure of DGG-B.

paragraphs.section:
Results and Discussion/Estimates of Cell Yields, Growth and Decay
Rates for Pseudomonas and ORM2
paragraphs.text: We performed mass and electron balances in each bottle to compare the ratios of donor (benzene) consumption to oxygen reduction (in aerobic phases) and to methane formation (in anoxic phases), including biomass formation. Cell yields were estimated from qPCR (16S rRNA gene copies/mL), cell size (g/copy), and benzene consumption data over each time interval; these calculations are detailed in Table S8. Although qPCR can overestimate cell copy numbers by capturing DNA from dead cells,52 we assumed this risk to be minimal since cell decay on the orders of magnitude was observed in this study. Measured values were compared to predictions shown in eq 1 (methanogenic case) and in eq 2 (aerobic case). In eq 2, the fraction of electrons from benzene going to cell synthesis was 50%, which is typical for aerobic processes.532

paragraphs.section:
Results and Discussion/Estimates of Cell Yields, Growth and Decay
Rates for Pseudomonas and ORM2
paragraphs.text: The average measured yield for Pseudomonas (∼1.1 g cells per g of benzene) during the aerobic phase was remarkably close to the predicted yield (Table 2). In contrast, the total yield of ORM2 and total Archaea under methanogenic conditions (∼0.04 g cells/g benzene) was found to be well below the predicted growth yield (0.22 g/g) shown in eq 1 and in Table 2. Low growth yields have been previously reported for this culture15,38 and are consistent with the difficulties commonly reported in trying to sustain high rates and cell concentrations in anaerobic benzene-degrading cultures.

paragraphs.section:
Results and Discussion/Estimates of Cell Yields, Growth and Decay
Rates for Pseudomonas and ORM2
paragraphs.text: To explore growth and decay rates more closely, we estimated net (i.e., measured) cell growth and decay rates for the two benzene degraders, Pseudomonas and ORM2 (Table S8), assuming first-order processes as an approximation. Using the slope from first-order regression of microbial abundance (from qPCR) vs time over specific intervals (aerobic, anaerobic), we were able to get some estimates that reflect observations in Bottles 1–5 (Table S8). In Table 2, we summarize the average and fastest rates estimated and provide calculated, representative doubling times or half-lives to make comparisons easier.

paragraphs.section:
Results and Discussion/Estimates of Cell Yields, Growth and Decay
Rates for Pseudomonas and ORM2
paragraphs.text: Growth rates for Pseudomonas were substantially faster than for ORM2, best seen in Table 2 by the difference in minimum/average doubling times (6/9 vs 26/66 days, respectively). These data are consistent with the literature and previous reports for ∼30 day doubling times for ORM2.15,38,43 As for observed decay rates, we see striking numbers for ORM2, particularly during aerobic phases, where the fastest decay rates and shortest half-lives of only 11 days were reported (Tables 2 and S8). This highlights a substantial loss of ORM2 biomass upon exposure to oxygen. The average half-life of ORM2 (calculated during aerobic and anaerobic periods of decay) was about 38 days, which is very short and incredibly close to the organism’s known doubling time. Therefore, it is not surprising that it took almost a year for the culture to recover. In previous experiments by Luo et al.,38 decay was essentially zero for ORM2 maintained anaerobically and without benzene. ORM2 is thus highly sensitive to oxygen and reinforces the existence of a novel, still unknown pathway independent of O2 in methanogenic benzene degradation.

paragraphs.section:
Results and Discussion/Impact of Oxygen on Other
Microbial Community Members
paragraphs.text: After realizing just how sensitive ORM2 is to oxygen, we were curious how other members of the DGG-B community responded to air addition events. Putative microbes represented by ASVs were divided into bacteria and Archaea and further categorized into one of the three groups: (i) ASVs that became enriched aerobically, (ii) ASVs that declined in response to O2 exposure, and (iii) ASVs that were largely unaffected (Figures S6a–d and S7a–d).

paragraphs.section:
Results and Discussion/Impact of Oxygen on Other
Microbial Community Members
paragraphs.text: Group 1 bacteria that were positively impacted by oxygen include the Pseudomonas ASV1 discussed above, as well as Sulfurferula ASV1, Thiomonas ASV1, and Rhizobium ASV1 (Figure S6a–c). None of these ASVs were detectable in anoxic control Bottles 4 and 5 at any time point (Figure S6d). Members of these genera are aerobic but can survive under anoxic conditions.48,54−56Sulfuriferula and Thiomonas are chemolithoautotrophs that oxidize some sulfur species (S0, thiosulfate, sulfide, and tetrathionate) with O2.55,56 Therefore, the FeS reducing agent in our growth medium could have supported the growth of Sulfuriferula or Thiomonas in the presence of O2. In our electron balance (Table S7), we assumed that the oxidation of FeS was abiotic, but these data suggest it may instead have been mediated by bacteria. Select rhizobial species can metabolize substituted aromatics, including phenol, a hydroxylated form of benzene that can be produced abiotically by autooxidation.19,54 Perhaps the bacterium associated with Rhizobium ASV1 served a similar role in the presence of oxygen.

paragraphs.section:
Results and Discussion/Impact of Oxygen on Other
Microbial Community Members
paragraphs.text: Group 2 microbes that were negatively impacted by oxygen include those we have already discussed: Deltaproteobacteria ASV1 (ORM2), two Ca. Nealsonbacteria ASVs (OD1), and Ca. Omnitrophica ASV1 (Figure S6a,b). High-abundance ASVs associated with Methanosaeta and Methanoregula also decreased 1–2 orders of magnitude following the addition of 10 mL air (Figure S7a,b). Concentrations of most of these bacterial and archaeal ASVs did not begin to recover until after ORM2 growth resumed and methanogenic benzene degradation was re-established. Notably, a few Group 2 ASVs in Bottles 1 and 2 never fully recovered from O2 exposure, including Ca. Nealsonbacteria ASV1 (Figure S6a,b), Methanoregula ASV2, and Methanosaeta ASV4 (Figure S7a,b), pointing to permanent community impacts.

paragraphs.section:
Results and Discussion/Impact of Oxygen on Other
Microbial Community Members
paragraphs.text: Group 3 comprises largely unimpacted microbes that were in low abundance and include two unclassified Spirochaetaceae ASVs, one ASV belonging to an unclassified Anaerolineaceae genus, and one ASV belonging to hydrogenotrophic Methanobacterium (Figures S6a–d and S7a–d). Spirochaetaceae and Anaerolineaceae are commonly detected in anaerobic and methanogenic hydrocarbon-degrading enrichment cultures, but their roles are often undefined. Some Spirochaetes are believed to mediate the recycling of biomass from dead cells.57Anaerolineceae are often closely associated with methanogens and may catalyze the degradation of other hydrocarbons.58,59 Our results suggest that the roles of group 3 microorganisms are independent of benzene degradation.

paragraphs.section: Results and Discussion/Implications for the Field
paragraphs.text: This study has made it abundantly clear that ORM2, the chief anaerobic benzene degrader in the DGG-B/OR consortium, is strictly anaerobic and oxygen-sensitive. Transient oxygen exposure contributed to extensive, prolonged decay of ORM2 and associated group 2 methanogens and putative biomass-recycling bacteria. A complete (closed) genome for ORM2 has been sequenced and is under investigation (JGI/IMG taxon ID 2795385393), but its biochemical mechanism for benzene transformation is still not known. Nevertheless, we can say for certain that oxygen is not involved in anaerobic benzene degradation by this culture and probably not in other consortia harboring ORM2-like benzene degraders.39−41

paragraphs.section: Results and Discussion/Implications for the Field
paragraphs.text: For years, our laboratory has wondered why anaerobic benzene degraders such as ORM2 rarely proliferate in subsurface benzene-contaminated environments. We recently explored environmental co-contaminants (i.e., toluene and xylenes) and microbial codependencies as possibilities constraining their growth15 but acknowledged that a multitude of other factors were likely involved. This study implicates transient oxygen exposure as another possibility. In the subsurface, dissolved oxygen may be introduced to anoxic zones from groundwater recharge, fluctuations in groundwater elevation, rain events, and diffusion from the vadose zone. Shallow unconfined aquifers are much more likely to see oxygen incursions. However, unlike our culture bottles, subsurface environments are highly heterogeneous and filled with microenvironments that would not see bulk oxygen concentrations. Nevertheless, careful attention to avoiding changes in redox potential appears warranted if sustained anaerobic benzene biotransformation is desired.

paragraphs.section: Results and Discussion/Implications for the Field
paragraphs.text: This study has also highlighted pronounced cell death/decay as another important factor constraining net microbial growth. Cell decay is often ignored in mathematical models, particularly in contaminant fate and transport models. It is frequently assumed that because anaerobic bacteria do not grow quickly, their decay rates must also be very low and can therefore be neglected. A rule of thumb is that decay rates are 1/10th of growth rates.53 Contrarily, we observed for ORM2 that growth and decay rates were of similar magnitude, even when oxygen was no longer present. This result is consistent with previously described challenges in achieving high cell densities and consistent benzene degradation rates in lab cultures. They could also help explain why organisms putatively associated with biomass recycling, including Ca. Nealsonbacteria (OD1) and Ca. Omnitrophica (OP3), among others, are periodically observed in high abundances in the DGG-B/OR consortium15,38 and other anaerobic benzene-degrading consortia.60,61 What factors could explain such relatively high decay rates? Possible explanations include viral and bacterial predation or microbial competition. Another explanation could be the formation of toxic reactive intermediates during benzene activation resulting in cell death or the energy penalty afforded by this difficult reaction. Understanding the underlying mechanisms of death and decay will be key to establishing more robust cultures for bioremediation. Interestingly, comparable methanogenic enrichment cultures that degrade toluene rather than benzene do not exhibit the same struggles and, thus, the most likely hypothesis is that a step in the biochemical activation of benzene contributes to higher rates of decay.
